sections.body:
This is a story about a girl called Linh. She wants to see the Moon for herself. Not in a book. Not on television. For herself.

She gets her chance on a clear winter night. A rocket stands on the launch pad, tall and white and full of fuel. Linh has a seat, a helmet and a list of things to do.

A good adventure has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who is going and why. The middle brings the surprise. The end gives you something worth keeping.

This trip has that shape. At the beginning, the rocket shakes on the pad and the whole sky is orange. In the middle, Linh floats in the dark and sees the Earth become a small blue ball. At the end, she stands on the Moon and finds something nobody expected.

Read it slowly. Then tell it to someone else. That is how an adventure becomes yours.
examples: This story is about a trip to the Moon.
A good adventure has a beginning, a middle and an end.
I can tell this story again tomorrow.
sections.heading: What this moon trip is about

sections.body:
The night is cold and clear. Stars sit low over the launch pad, and everybody is bundled up.

Linh sits in a small seat high inside the rocket. The seat is a **seat belt** on its own, because there is no gravity to hold her down. She pulls it tight over her chest. Her hands shake a little.

The voice on the radio counts backwards. Ten. Nine. Eight. Nobody says a word. The whole crowd knows the numbers by heart.

Then the engine wakes up. It roars so loudly that Linh feels it in her teeth, not just her ears. Fire and steam come out from the bottom of the rocket, and the ground shakes under it.

Slowly, the rocket lifts. The launch pad gets smaller. The trees get smaller. Soon the pad is only a bright dot in a big dark field.

Linh does not look back. She watches the sky turn from blue to black, and she counts her own breaths.
examples: The launch pad got smaller and smaller.
The engine roared so loudly that she felt it in her teeth.
She counted her own breaths all the way up.
sections.heading: How the trip began

sections.body:
Up in the sky, everything gets strange. The loud roar stops, and the silence is so big that it feels like a sound of its own.

Linh is **weightless**. That means she does not feel heavy at all. Her pencil floats away and hangs in the air. Her hair stands up. If she lets go of a sandwich, it does not fall. It just drifts.

She watches the Earth through the small round window. At first the ocean is blue and the clouds are white. Then the whole planet fits inside the window, and it looks like a marble made of water.

They pass the Moon and go around it. That long loop around the Moon is called an **orbit**. Linh counts the loops on her list and writes the number down.

The ship turns slowly. Through the window, the Moon comes closer. It is grey and round and full of holes. Those holes are called **craters**. They are made by rocks that hit the Moon a very long time ago.

The radio crackles. The captain says the landing lights are on. Linh holds her list with both hands and gets ready.
examples: Everything floated in the ship, even her pencil.
The Earth looked like a small blue marble.
The Moon was grey and full of craters.
sections.heading: The middle: the long ride through the dark

sections.body:
The rocket touches down softly. No cloud of dust. No big shake. The Moon has no wind, and no wind means no dust to blow around.

Linh climbs down the ladder and puts her boot on the surface for the first time. It makes a footprint. A real footprint, sharp and clear.

Then she tries to jump. She pushes hard, and she flies up higher than she expected. She comes down slowly, like a feather. On the Earth she would fall in a second. Here she takes her time, and she laughs out loud.

She walks to a big crater and looks at the rocks around it. One small grey rock has a strange mark on it. She photographs it. Later, scientists on Earth will study the picture and say the rock is older than the dinosaurs. Older than almost everything we know.

But the surprise is not the rock. The surprise is what Linh finds back inside the ship, in her pocket. When she left Earth, she put one small thing there. A folded paper star, made by her grandmother.

She thought it would be lost in the black sky. It was in her pocket the whole time. Some things you carry to the far side and bring home safe.
examples: Her boot made a sharp footprint in the grey dust.
She jumped high and came down slowly, like a feather.
The paper star was in her pocket the whole time.
sections.heading: The surprise: the rock that nobody expected

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in this story. Learn them here, and you can use them in your own sentences.

A **rocket** is a machine that pushes itself up into the sky with fire and gas. A **launch pad** is the platform where the rocket stands before it flies.

An **astronaut** is a person trained to fly into space. Astronauts wear a spacesuit so they can breathe in places where there is no air.

Weightlessness is the feeling of floating, with nothing pulling you down. **Orbit** is the long loop a spacecraft travels around the Moon or the Earth.

A **crater** is a round hollow in the ground. On the Moon, craters were made by rocks that fell from space long ago.
examples: A rocket needs fire and gas to fly.
The crater was made by a rock from space.
sections.heading: The words inside this story

terms.example: The rocket stood on the pad, white and tall.
terms.gloss: A machine that pushes itself up into the sky with fire and gas. It is how people reach space.

terms.example: Everybody watched from the launch pad.
terms.gloss: The platform where the rocket stands and waits before it flies.

terms.example: The astronaut opened the hatch and stepped out.
terms.gloss: A person trained to fly into space. Astronauts wear a spacesuit because there is no air out there.

terms.example: In weightlessness, even a pencil can float.
terms.gloss: The feeling of floating, with nothing pulling you down. Everything drifts in the ship.

terms.example: They went around the Moon in an orbit.
terms.gloss: The long loop a spacecraft travels around the Moon or the Earth.

sections.body:
What did Linh learn? She learned that the far side of the sky is not the empty place people say it is. It has grey dust, sharp footprints, a very old rock and a whole world turning underneath her.

She also learned something quieter. The paper star travelled all the way to the Moon in her pocket. She did not need to hold it tight. She only needed to keep it with her.

Here is how to tell this adventure to someone. Keep the order, and the surprise will land in the right place.

Start with who is going and why. Tell the hard part in the middle. Save the surprise for last. Then say the small lesson in one short sentence.

The lesson of this adventure is this: the biggest places look small when you are ready to go and look.
examples: The story starts with a countdown at the launch pad.
The surprise comes at the very end.
Big places look small when you are ready to go and look.
sections.heading: The small lesson, and how to tell the story
steps: Start with the character: Linh at the launch pad, waiting for the countdown.
Tell the middle: the long silent ride, the floating ship and the grey Moon.
Tell the surprise: the old rock, and the paper star that came home.
End with the lesson: big places look small when you are ready to go.

item.summary: A girl climbs into a rocket and flies all the way to the Moon. Follow her through the countdown, the long dark sky and the quiet grey surface. After reading, you can retell the trip, use five new space words in your own sentences, and explain why the Moon feels light and bouncy.
item.title: A Trip to the Moon
